what_its_for: Desvenlafaxine is used to treat major depressive disorder (MDD) in adults. It helps improve your mood, energy level, sleep, and appetite, and reduces feelings of sadness, anxiety, and worthlessness. It belongs to a class of medicines called serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs), which work by balancing certain natural chemicals in the brain.
how_to_take: Take desvenlafaxine by mouth once a day, with or without food. Swallow the tablet whole — do not crush, chew, split, or dissolve it. Take it at the same time each day to help you remember. You may notice a ghost tablet (empty shell) in your stool — this is normal and does not mean the medicine did not work.
dosing: The usual starting and maintenance dose is 50 mg once daily. Your doctor may adjust your dose based on how you respond to the medicine. Do not take more or less than your doctor prescribed. Do not stop taking this medicine suddenly without talking to your doctor first, as this can cause withdrawal symptoms such as dizziness, nausea, headache, and irritability. Your doctor will slowly lower your dose before you stop completely.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — unless it is almost time for your next scheduled dose. In that case, skip the missed dose and take your next dose at the regular time. Never take two doses at once to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store desvenlafaxine at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C and 25°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep this medicine out of reach of children and pets. Dispose of any unused or expired medication safely — ask your pharmacist about a local drug take-back program.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking desvenlafaxine, as it can increase side effects like dizziness and drowsiness. Do not take monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) — such as phenelzine, tranylcypromine, or linezolid — within 14 days of taking desvenlafaxine, as this combination can cause a serious and life-threatening reaction. Be careful when driving or operating heavy machinery until you know how this medicine affects you. Avoid taking other medicines for depression, migraine, or pain without checking with your doctor or pharmacist first, as they may interact with desvenlafaxine.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the nearest emergency room if you experience: thoughts of suicide or self-harm, unusual changes in behavior or mood, signs of serotonin syndrome (agitation, hallucinations, fast heartbeat, fever, muscle stiffness or twitching, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea), signs of high blood pressure (severe headache, vision changes, chest pain), unusual bleeding or bruising, seizures, or severe allergic reaction (rash, swelling of the face or throat, difficulty breathing). Contact your doctor if you have persistent nausea, trouble sleeping, sexual problems, or if you feel your depression is getting worse.
when_it_works: Desvenlafaxine does not work right away. You may start to notice some improvement in sleep, appetite, and energy within the first 1 to 2 weeks. However, it may take 4 to 8 weeks of regular use before you feel the full benefit of this medicine. Be patient and continue taking it even if you do not feel better right away. Do not stop taking it without talking to your doctor.
special_populations: Pregnant women: Talk to your doctor before taking this medicine if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Taking desvenlafaxine late in pregnancy may cause temporary withdrawal symptoms in the newborn. Breastfeeding: This medicine passes into breast milk. Talk to your doctor about the risks and benefits before breastfeeding. Older adults (65+): You may be more sensitive to side effects such as dizziness and falls. Use with care and talk to your doctor about the right dose. Kidney or liver problems: Your doctor may need to adjust your dose if you have moderate to severe kidney or liver disease. Children and teenagers: Desvenlafaxine is not approved for use in people under 18 years old. Antidepressants may increase the risk of suicidal thoughts in children and young adults — monitor closely for any changes in mood or behavior.
